title: Smoked Ricotta Gnocchi with Sage Butter
summary: This delicate Italian dumpling course offers an unforgettable taste experience centered around a distinct smoked element. Whole milk ricotta cheese is cold-smoked over sweet applewood chips before being folded with egg yolks, freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano, nutmeg, and type 00 flour. The resulting tender gnocchi dumplings melt in your mouth, carrying a subtle whisper of woodsmoke that elevates the classic dish. Gently poached in salted water, the dumplings are tossed in a golden brown butter sauce crispy with fresh garden sage leaves and toasted hazelnuts. A squeeze of fresh lemon juice cuts through the rich butter while cracked black pepper adds warmth. Elegant enough for a formal dinner party yet simple to prepare, this dish beautifully marries rustic mountain woodfire notes with refined Italian pasta craftsmanship. Rich in calcium, high-quality dairy protein, and comforting flavors, this plate brings cozy luxury to any dining table.

steps.step: Line a fine mesh strainer with cheesecloth and place whole milk ricotta inside to drain excess whey.
Let ricotta drain over a bowl in refrigerator for two hours until very firm and dry.
Set up stovetop smoker with applewood chips according to manufacturer instructions.
Spread drained ricotta across shallow foil pan and cold-smoke over low heat for fifteen minutes.
Remove smoked ricotta from smoker and let cool completely at room temperature.
Grate fresh Parmigiano-Reggiano and Pecorino Romano finely using microplane grater.
Separate two egg yolks from whites into a small glass bowl, discarding egg whites.
Grate fresh whole nutmeg using microplane into small spice pinch dish.
Coarsely chop toasted hazelnuts into crunchy medium pieces on cutting board.
Wash fresh sage leaves gently under cold water and pat completely dry with paper towel.
Zest fresh lemon finely with microplane and squeeze one tablespoon juice into cup.
Mince small shallot finely to add subtle aromatic base to brown butter sauce later.
Dust clean rimmed baking sheet generously with semolina flour to receive shaped gnocchi.
Measure out type 00 flour carefully, sifting it through fine strainer into bowl.
Set out white truffle oil, balsamic reduction, and flaky sea salt near plating station.
Prepare large pot filled with four quarts of fresh cold water for boiling gnocchi.
Cover workspace with clean parchment paper for shaping and cutting tender gnocchi ropes.
Chop fresh parsley and chives finely, storing herbs together in small chilled cup.
Verify smoked ricotta has cooled completely before mixing into dumpling dough mix.
Organize all prepped ingredients, tools, and utensils cleanly near main cooking stove.
Fill large bowl with ice water to set up cold bath if pre-chilling cooked dumplings.
Place cooled smoked ricotta into large stainless steel mixing bowl for dough preparation.
Add egg yolks, grated Parmigiano-Reggiano, nutmeg, sea salt, and white pepper to ricotta.
Stir ricotta mixture gently with rubber spatula until completely smooth and unified.
Sift half of type 00 flour over ricotta mix, folding gently with light touch.
Sift remaining flour over dough, mixing just until flour disappears into soft dough.
Be careful not to overwork gnocchi dough to preserve light tender dumpling texture.
Dust work surface lightly with type 00 flour and turn dough out gently onto surface.
Divide dough into four equal quarter portions using bench scraper tool cleanly.
Roll one dough portion gently under palms into long three-quarter-inch thick rope.
Cut rope into three-quarter-inch individual gnocchi pillows using floured bench scraper.
Roll each cut dumpling lightly over tines of gnocchi board to form classic ridges.
Transfer shaped smoked ricotta gnocchi onto semolina-dusted baking sheet in single layer.
Repeat rolling and cutting process for remaining three portions of tender ricotta dough.
Ensure shaped gnocchi do not touch each other on baking sheet to prevent sticking.
Dust top of shaped gnocchi lightly with extra semolina flour for protective coating.
Refrigerate shaped gnocchi for fifteen minutes to help them hold shape during boiling.
Check that all dumplings are uniform in size to guarantee even cooking in water.
Keep extra type 00 flour nearby in case dough feels too sticky during shaping phase.
Wipe work counter clean of flour dust while gnocchi chill briefly in refrigerator.
Bring large pot of salted water to rolling boil over high heat on stovetop burner.
Prepare wide skillet on adjacent burner for creating crispy sage brown butter sauce.
Add two tablespoons of kosher salt into boiling water pot, stirring to dissolve fully.
Melt six tablespoons of unsalted butter in wide skillet over medium heat until bubbling.
Add minced shallot, garlic cloves, and fresh sage leaves into melting pan butter.
Cook butter mixture for three minutes until butter solids turn nutty golden brown color.
Carefully transfer half of chilled smoked ricotta gnocchi into boiling water pot.
Stir boiling water gently once with wooden spoon so gnocchi do not stick to bottom.
Cook gnocchi until they float up to surface of boiling water, about two minutes.
Allow floating gnocchi to simmer for thirty seconds more to ensure centers are hot.
Use slotted spider utensil to transfer floating gnocchi directly into brown butter skillet.
Drop remaining batch of chilled gnocchi carefully into boiling water pot to cook.
Remove crispy sage leaves from skillet onto paper towel plate, leaving brown butter in pan.
Stir second batch of floating gnocchi into brown butter skillet once fully cooked.
Pour in quarter cup of starchy pasta cooking water into brown butter skillet to emulsify.
Add lemon juice, lemon zest, white wine, and heavy cream to skillet, tossing gently.
Swirl skillet over medium heat for one minute until sauce coats gnocchi in glossy sheen.
Stir in baby spinach leaves until just wilted around warm brown butter dumpling mix.
Taste butter sauce carefully and adjust seasoning with smoked salt and red pepper flakes.
Turn off stove heat under gnocchi skillet once sauce is silky and perfectly bound.
Ensure smoked ricotta dumplings remain whole and delicate without breaking in sauce.
Warm shallow pasta bowls in 150 degree oven for five minutes before final plating.
Prepare tongs and warm serving spoon for elegant portioning into individual bowls.
Ladle smoked ricotta gnocchi and brown butter sauce evenly among four warm pasta bowls.
Arrange tender dumplings neatly in center of each bowl, spooning pan reduction over.
Top each bowl with reserved crispy sage leaves for striking green color contrast.
Scatter coarsely chopped toasted hazelnuts over gnocchi for delightful crunchy bite.
Grate extra Parmigiano-Reggiano and Pecorino Romano cheese over warm dumplings generously.
Drizzle light drops of white truffle oil and balsamic reduction around rim of bowls.
Garnish each portion with chopped fresh parsley, chives, and light pinch of nutmeg.
Finish each plate with sprinkle of flaky sea salt and freshly cracked black pepper.
Wipe bowl rims clean with damp paper towel before carrying dishes to dining table.
Serve immediately while gnocchi are piping hot and brown butter sauce is aromatic.
Pair with crisp Italian Pinot Grigio or light Nebbiolo wine to balance smoked ricotta.
Encourage guests to enjoy delicate texture and subtle woodsmoke flavor in each bite.
Offer extra grated cheese and fresh pepper mill at table for individual guest preferences.
Enjoy sophisticated harmony of applewood smoke, brown butter, and crisp fried sage leaves.
Clear bowls easily as guests finish every pillowy bite of this special dumpling dish.
Store any unboiled leftover gnocchi frozen on baking sheet before packing into bags.
Boil frozen gnocchi straight from freezer in salted water, adding one minute cook time.
Store leftover brown butter sauce in small jar in fridge for up to four days.
Reheat leftover sauce gently in small saucepan over low flame before drizzling on pasta.
Celebrate artisanal Italian pasta making techniques enhanced by delicate wood smoking.
Conclude elegant dinner course with refreshing citrus sorbet or espresso coffee service.
